q-138488.name: Question 1
q-138488.problem:
For the matrix 
$A=[\begin{aligned}4 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 & 0\end{aligned}],$ find the pseudoinverse ${A}^{+}.$
q-138488.worked_solution:
For an "almost" zero $m\times n$ matrix with non-zero entries 

$$
{\sigma }_{1},\,{\sigma }_{2},\,…,\,{\sigma }_{r}
$$

on the main diagonal, the corresponding pseudoinverse is the "almost" zero $n\times m$ matrix with entries 

$$
{\sigma }_{1}^{-1},\,{\sigma }_{2}^{-1},\,…,\,{\sigma }_{r}^{-1}
$$

on the main diagonal.

Therefore, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{+} & ={[\begin{aligned}4 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 & 0\end{aligned}]}^{+} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{4}^{-1} & 0 \\ 0 & {3}^{-1} \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{12}[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 4 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

For the matrix A=[400030], find the pseudoinverse A+.

a
112[300040]
b
112[004003]
c
112[300400]
d
112[−400300]
e
112[400030]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

For an "almost" zero m×n matrix with non-zero entries

σ1,σ2,…,σr

on the main diagonal, the corresponding pseudoinverse is the "almost" zero n×m matrix with entries

σ1−1,σ2−1,…,σr−1

on the main diagonal.

Therefore, we obtain

A+=[400030]+=[4−1003−100]=112[300400].

q-138493.problem:
For the matrix 
$A=[\begin{aligned}6 & 0 \\ 0 & -9 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}],$ find the pseudoinverse ${A}^{+}.$
q-138493.worked_solution:
For an "almost" zero $m\times n$ matrix with non-zero entries 

$$
{\sigma }_{1},\,{\sigma }_{2},\,…,\,{\sigma }_{r}
$$

on the main diagonal, the corresponding pseudoinverse is the "almost" zero $n\times m$ matrix with entries 

$$
{\sigma }_{1}^{-1},\,{\sigma }_{2}^{-1},\,…,\,{\sigma }_{r}^{-1}
$$

on the main diagonal.

Therefore, we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{+} & ={[\begin{aligned}6 & 0 \\ 0 & -9 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]}^{+} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{6}^{-1} & \,\,\,0 & 0 \\ \,\,0 & \,(-9)^{-1} & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{18}[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -2 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Question 2
?

For the matrix A=[600−900], find the pseudoinverse A+.

a
118[3000−20]
b
−19[300020]
c
118[2000−30]
d
16[−300020]
e
19[300020]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

For an "almost" zero m×n matrix with non-zero entries

σ1,σ2,…,σr

on the main diagonal, the corresponding pseudoinverse is the "almost" zero n×m matrix with entries

σ1−1,σ2−1,…,σr−1

on the main diagonal.

Therefore, we obtain

A+=[600−900]+=[6−1000(−9)−10]=118[3000−20].

q-136972.name: Question 3
q-136972.problem:
$$
U=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} & 0 & \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} & 0 & \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \\ 0 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}],\,Σ=[\begin{aligned}5 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}],\,V=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} & \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrices shown above. Given that $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of $A,$ find the pseudoinverse ${A}^{+}.$
q-136972.worked_solution:
If $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of $A,$ then the pseudoinverse of $A$ is given by

$$
V\,{Σ}^{+}\,{U}^{T},
$$

where ${Σ}^{+}$ is the pseudoinverse of $Σ.$

First, notice that

$$
V=\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}-1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}],\,{Σ}^{+}=\frac{1}{5}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}],\,{U}^{T}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}-1 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & \sqrt{5} \\ 2 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{+} & =V\,{Σ}^{+}\,{U}^{T} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}-1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{5}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}-1 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & \sqrt{5} \\ 2 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{25}[\begin{aligned}-1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}-1 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & \sqrt{5} \\ 2 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{25}[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 & 0 \\ 2 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}-1 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & \sqrt{5} \\ 2 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{25}[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 0 \\ -2 & 4 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

q-138516.name: Question 4
q-138516.problem:
$$
U=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}],\,Σ=[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}],\,V=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrices shown above. Given that $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of $A,$ find the pseudoinverse ${A}^{+}.$
q-138516.worked_solution:
If $A=UΣ{V}^{T}$ is a singular value decomposition of $A,$ then the pseudoinverse of $A$ is given by

$$
V\,{Σ}^{+}\,{U}^{T},
$$

where ${Σ}^{+}$ is the pseudoinverse of $Σ.$

First, notice that

$$
V=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}],\,{Σ}^{+}=\frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}],\,{U}^{T}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{+} & =V\,{Σ}^{+}\,{U}^{T} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{2}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{4}[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{4}[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{4}[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

q-136992.name: Question 5
q-136992.problem:
$$
{U}_{r}=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{3\sqrt{2}} & -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{4}{3\sqrt{2}} & 0 \\ -\frac{1}{3\sqrt{2}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}],\,{Σ}_{r}=[\begin{aligned}6 & 0 \\ 0 & 4\end{aligned}],\,{V}_{r}=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & -\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrices shown above. Given that $A={U}_{r}{Σ}_{r}{V}_{r}^{T}$ is a reduced singular value decomposition of $A,$ find the pseudoinverse ${A}^{+}.$
q-136992.worked_solution:
If $A={U}_{r}{Σ}_{r}{V}_{r}^{T}$ is a reduced singular value decomposition of $A,$ then the pseudoinverse of $A$ is given by

$$
{V}_{r}\,{Σ}_{r}^{+}\,{U}_{r}^{T},
$$

where ${Σ}_{r}^{+}$ is the pseudoinverse of ${Σ}_{r}.$

First, notice that

$$
{V}_{r}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}],\,{Σ}_{r}^{+}=\frac{1}{24}[\begin{aligned}4 & 0 \\ 0 & 6\end{aligned}],\,{U}_{r}^{T}=\frac{1}{3\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}-1 & 4 & -1 \\ -3 & 0 & 3\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{+} & ={V}_{r}\,{Σ}_{r}^{+}\,{U}_{r}^{T} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{24}[\begin{aligned}4 & 0 \\ 0 & 6\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{3\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}-1 & 4 & -1 \\ -3 & 0 & 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{144}[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}4 & 0 \\ 0 & 6\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}-1 & 4 & -1 \\ -3 & 0 & 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{144}[\begin{aligned}4 & -6 \\ 4 & 6\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}-1 & 4 & -1 \\ -3 & 0 & 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{144}[\begin{aligned}14 & 16 & -22 \\ -22 & 16 & 14\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{72}[\begin{aligned}7 & 8 & -11 \\ -11 & 8 & 7\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

q-138621.problem:
$$
{U}_{r}=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} & -\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ 0 & 0 \\ \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\end{aligned}],\,{Σ}_{r}=[\begin{aligned}10 & 0 \\ 0 & 5\end{aligned}],\,{V}_{r}=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} & \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ -\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrices shown above. Given that $A={U}_{r}{Σ}_{r}{V}_{r}^{T}$ is a reduced singular value decomposition of $A,$ find the pseudoinverse ${A}^{+}.$
q-138621.worked_solution:
If $A={U}_{r}{Σ}_{r}{V}_{r}^{T}$ is a reduced singular value decomposition of $A,$ then the pseudoinverse of $A$ is given by

$$
{V}_{r}\,{Σ}_{r}^{+}\,{U}_{r}^{T},
$$

where ${Σ}_{r}^{+}$ is the pseudoinverse of ${Σ}_{r}.$

First, notice that

$$
{V}_{r}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}],\,{Σ}_{r}^{+}=\frac{1}{10}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}],\,{U}_{r}^{T}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 2 \\ -2 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{+} & ={V}_{r}\,{Σ}_{r}^{+}\,{U}_{r}^{T} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{10}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 2 \\ -2 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{50}[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 2 \\ -2 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{50}[\begin{aligned}1 & 4 \\ -2 & 2\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 2 \\ -2 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{50}[\begin{aligned}-7 & 0 & 6 \\ -6 & 0 & -2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

a
150[−20660−7]

150[60−7−206]

150[−706−60−2]
e
150[0−7606−2]

EXPLANATION

If A=UrΣrVrT is a reduced singular value decomposition of A, then the pseudoinverse of A is given by

VrΣr+UrT,

where Σr+ is the pseudoinverse of Σr.

First, notice that

Vr=15[12−21],Σr+=110[1002],UrT=15[102−201].

A+=VrΣr+UrT=15[12−21]⋅110[1002]⋅15[102−201]=150[12−21]⋅[1002]⋅[102−201]=150[14−22]⋅[102−201]=150[−706−60−2].
